RT @cr3ghost: SMB signing enforced? You might still be vulnerable to relay.

Really interesting research from @aas_s3curity demonstrating how SMB2/3 re-authentication can bypass enforced signing on affected Windows systems, potentially including Domain Controllers.

The technique:

• Establish an SMB session using a low-privileged account
• Relay privileged NTLM or Kerberos authentication
• Re-authenticate the existing session as that identity
• Abuse retention of the original signing key
• Access the privileged session while signing with a key you control

The underlying issue is a missing identity check during re-authentication.

The author released reauthx, a krbrelayx fork, alongside tooling to identify affected hosts.

Important: September 2026 Windows updates appear to address this. Successful exploitation still requires a suitable privileged authentication and other relay preconditions.

Excellent research building on work from Dirk-jan Mollema, Synacktiv, SySS, Semperis and SpecterOps.

items.content:
RT @hillelogram: It is a weird weird year to be a formal methods expert.

Some unorganized thoughts on the new @AnthropicAI and @theoremlabs post on formal verification (https://t.co/YoymKXYFJa):

- This is very cool.

- The main innovation is verifying a later stage of the program. Normally provers take the source code, LLM it into a theorem language, and then prove that, which means you have to make assumptions about source semantics and compilation properties. It's very easy to make a mistake in translating and prove the wrong thing! 

What they instead do is compile the code into assembly, and then (if I understand this correctly), compile that assembly into a theorem language (which they call LPS). So as long as the compiler is faithful you can skip the whole divergence problem.

- I'm glad they clarify that you still have to trust the translation process, the "hardware, OS, OCaml" compiler, the LPS model, and also assume that the program is single threaded with fixed memory. The single biggest source of errors in formally verified code is when the proof assumes something that isn't true in practice. It's really, really important to state your assumptions!

- I'm not clear why they need to compile the fuzzer into the theorem. Is it to act as a description of valid inputs and workload? Maybe to embed assertions in as theorems?

- Holy crap, 180 million lines of Rocq. Is that more Rocq than exists in the world already? I notice they say a 600,000 line proof corresponds to roughly 20k CPU instructions. That would be like, 1-2k lines of source code at most? Really goes to show how inefficient this approach is and how it only works because you can throw LLMs at the problem.

- This, probably deliberately, doesn't address the single biggest gap in AI-based verification: AIs cannot come up with good properties. Doesn't matter if you're doing unit testing, property testing, formal verification. I always assumed this was a "frontier labs haven't trained for it yet" thing, but if Anthropic hasn't talked about that here, maybe they've tried and haven't been successful yet. That's interesting to me.

Instead, they take a known universal property (this code doesn't crash or get flagged by UBsan) and prove that instead. Still very useful, but makes it harder to generalize to proving arbitrary things about arbitrary programs.

- Anybody reading the official post should also read their expert review appendix (https://t.co/qQU0E0nJwW). It points out some interesting things, like the fact that most of the code the LLM wrote wasn't used in the proof (over one billion lines of Rocq), that they had to prove the equivalence between fuzzed and unfuzzed programs, and (this is most interesting), some experiments find that the LLM-method of proofwriting may not scale to more complex things.

- Also read the description of LPS (https://t.co/hRTCL05X0H) to understand the limitations of the assembly -> Rocq compilation. In particular, it does not handle concurrency at all (which is one of the main use cases for formal methods!) or OS signals. Also it can't prove things about program arguments with slash characters, meaning they can prove stuff about `rm foo` but not `rm foo/bar`.

- The official skill (https://t.co/weDOdmJUfO) doesn't tell us much about the nature of FM and AI. Probably too much for me to hope of any skill.

- Some of the article's specific caveats and throat clearings make me think someone at Anthropic reads my stuff ( ͡° ͜ʖ ͡°)

items.content:
RT @lorenc_dan: The actual prompt for this was "let's look for pre-auth RCEs in PHP". I'm sharing this so people know this stuff is real and to take agent-assisted scanning seriously.

I kicked if off using Claude Mythos 5.1 (in stock Claude Code) but it uses a skill to drive a harness we built over the last few months.

I don't know if the harness is amazing, but it certainly has a scary track record so far. It's setup to do an agent guided tree search across a codebase, and runs in microvm sandboxes that all have the full source code for the target, as well as the source for any transitive dependencies.

When I built the harness I basically just fed Claude a bunch of Project Zero blog posts describing how they did research and had it build a harness that ran like that, but on our tech stack.

The first phase is just setup and can run with any model, it just does that fetching and assembles the kit environment, and gets a target up and running alongside the source code.

Then we just do some basic suspend/resume stuff over to the hunt phase, where one agent supervises the tree, and the first node kicks off.

Each node is context-aware and aware of the work of all the others. I think I ran this with parallelism 4? So 4 running at any one time. The supervisor can shape the tree and boost nodes or prune. Any node can add more below it with targeted instructions.

A typical run looks like the first node doing a codebase review or building and running a fuzzer or something, all depending on the target. Then based on whatever it finds, it'll queue 4-5 children that go look into those areas. The main system guidance is to validate everything 3 times in clean VMs, and we typically require full exploit chains/POCs.

Here's what this run looked like.

We're doing this with a bunch of other open source projects now and companies. We're doing a lot of this for free, even with private companies, across critical infrastructure. We're directly partnered with Anthropic, and can do this even if you don't have direct access to a frontier model yourself.

items.content:
RT @MalwareTechBlog: I'll be the first to admit I'm mediocre at exploit development, but I am in contact with enough extremely talented exploit developers to say this for certain:

Anyone claiming they were "easily" able to generate a working php2shell exploit with AI is either:

a) a world-class exploit developer with an extreme case of imposter syndrome.

b) currently looking at some very confident-sounding but wrong LLM output.

I'm rather certain it's the latter based on the number of AI-hallucinated exploits I've seen posted on GitHub. Threat actors are also blasting my honeypot network with "php2shell" exploits that not only don't work, but aren't even within 10,000 miles of anything to do with how the exploit actually works.

I've seen the same technique from the attached image in multiple alleged "php2shell exploits", including one on GitHub with over 100 stars. Problem is, it's not php2shell, nor is it even a vulnerability at all. It's a technique known as "session poisoning", which can be leveraged to exploit local file inclusion (LFI) vulnerabilities in PHP apps (not PHP itself).

The only thing it has in common with CVE-2026-109618/CVE-2026-109619 is they both use the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" feature. And mitigation advice for both issues reference setting "session.upload_progress.enabled" to "Off".

People are shoving loose details of the vulnerability into LLMs, the LLMs are keying in on the "PHP_SESSION_UPLOAD_PROGRESS" string, then generating session poisoning code that has nothing to do with the actual CVE. And because the people doing this have absolutely no idea what they're doing, they're confident enough to post their "proof of concept exploit" to GitHub and share it on social media.

So if you see people talking about "session poisoning + LFI" it's likely their LLM hallucinated an exploit based on a 2018 blog by Orange Tsai talking about a local file inclusion attack vector.

What's even worse is that "security researchers" are then using LLMs to triage these exploitation attempts, falling victim to the same hallucinations, then confirming there is ongoing mass-exploitation (there currently isn't).

The actual real exploit is very difficult to exploit, and so far I've not seen anyone successfully get it working on more than a handful of PHP version with highly-specific configurations.

LLMs are useful tools in the hands of skilled professionals, but for others, they're often just a Dunning-Kruger accelerator.

uhm... i think this seems like the wrong approach, especially if the goal is to formally verify every piece of software we have and eliminate every bug, we should definitely formally verify lots of software but "everything"???

first of all, how do you even deal with state explosion and the sheer complexity of real world software and its dependencies? are you really sure mythos 8 or gpt-8 won't find flaws in your proofs, specs, or assumptions? how do you even specify the behavior of nondeterministic agents, especially you have to balanced against usability?

i don't think the goal should be eliminating vulnerabilities or proving their absence. that's not going to happen at the scale and complexity of real world software.

start by assuming vulnerabilities are inevitable, then build around that assumption. reduce attack surfaces, isolate critical systems, and make exploitation as difficult as possible.

i think thinking cyber is just fixing vulnerabilities might not be a great idea.

items.content:
This is 100% correct when looking at it from a single-system perspective. ASLR does not create a significant barrier to successful exploitation. But when looking at it from a mass-exploitation perspective, there are a lot of hidden complexities that come into play.

Vulnerability research is one of the few fields where you tend to make more money on the right side of the law. There isn't a huge demand for black market exploits. Most of the money is in bug bounty, working as a vulnerability researcher, or selling to grey-market exploit brokers.

This means that even the smallest bit of added complexity can take a vulnerability from 'cybercriminal free-for-all' to 'unlikely to be widely exploited'. 

Mass-exploitation events are almost always preceded by someone publishing fully-weaponized point-and-click exploit code. It's extremely rare for criminal groups to successfully develop exploit for higher-complexity vulnerabilities on their own, even with AI.

So, less researchers capable of exploiting the bug means less chance of a working weaponized exploit being posted online. But also, the increased difficulty of exploitation, thus increased time/effort, discourages those who can exploit the bug from giving it away for free.

There's also per-target variability (which I don't know for sure is the case with this bug). But with more complex bugs, it'll sometimes be impossible to make universal exploits. In extreme cases, attackers may need to build exploit for each specific system or software version, or each specific config, or maybe even both.

So, while it's correct that it's not hard to find an ASLR bypass, it is difficult to find a bypass that works reliably at scale. So far, most of the working exploits I've seen are limited to just a handful of PHP versions, or bruteforcing ASLR. And that makes all the difference when it comes to the risk of threat actors spraying exploits at the entire internet.

For this specific exploit, the honest answer is, I don't know. It's above my pay grade. But I'm almost 100% certain that the level of bad this will be will be directly dependent on what kind of exploits security researchers make public.

I think this is more serious than many people realize.

Not every Node.js server is vulnerable, of course. The application needs to process untrusted Brotli-compressed data.

But how common is that? Well, common middleware configurations in Express 5 can already expose the vulnerable decoder, without developers explicitly using Brotli anywhere in their code.

So we’re potentially looking at a pretty large attack surface, although nobody really knows how many deployments are exploitable yet.

I wouldn’t be surprised to see automated scanning and exploitation attempts targeting this very soon.

Patch your Node.js runtimes.

RT @joshua_saxe: Thoughts on php2shell and the overall looming crisis in cybersecurity

If you'd been appropriately pricing in that we'd see this and many more celebrity zero-days at an increasing rate, this is a positive update; defenders found this issue, alongside tens of thousands of others in the last year, before widespread exploitation, and it's being patched.

Real attackers will exploit this, but we shouldn't expect a recognizable blip in overall cyber damages in the next couple quarters, because easier initial access to victim networks wasn't a core bottleneck for attackers, and because defenders are better positioned to adopt AI automation than attackers, and are doing so faster; this advantage will persist through at least H1 2027, and possibly longer, IMO.

Why I think this: consider that, in general and on average, defenders have access to default-world capital networks and AI talent, often as a function of how central they are to Internet and societal infrastructure.  They have consistent, reliable access to AI inference from open- and closed-weight providers.

Criminal attackers, on the other hand, face the threat of arrest, difficulty accessing AI talent, and unreliable access to AI inference.  They're competing for and attempting to retain talent willing to risk arrest and sanctions, and willing to live a life of crime.

Nation-state attackers, meanwhile, operate within military and intelligence bureaucracies that have historically lagged private industry in adopting technologies, from mobile devices to drones.  Non-US-aligned nation-state attackers also face challenges in reliably, consistently, and secretly accessing US frontier models.

So, all in all, AI is making offensive capabilities cheaper, but that doesn't immediately translate into damages.  At this point, this is a robust finding from the entire 2022–26 period; as in the rest of the economy, we haven't seen a big AI-driven productivity bump among attackers, and attackers are even more disadvantaged than your average business or civilian state agency.

Of course, this won't last forever!  How do we exploit our current, limited defense-dominant window?  Getting to a good-enough steady state will require creative thinking.  I liked @chrisrohlf's piece on eliminating attack surface in OSS applications because it identifies leverage points for eliminating whole classes of risk using 2026-era AI (https://t.co/L2alFLbNs9).

We also need to revisit formal verification, control flow integrity, dynamic taint tracking, and the like, now that AI can make them more practical than they used to be.  We also have an enormous overhang of underdeployed defensive technology.  Honeypots, honeytokens, sandboxing, multi-factor authentication, and application allowlisting are all less widely deployed than they should be because businesses calculated they weren't worth it.

The AI industry should recognize that heavily gated trusted access programs have failed as a strategy; php2shell was identified by defenders first, and we need more defenders identifying more bugs faster.  The defense-dominant window is exactly the moment to pour gas on the fire of diffusion of as-cheap-as-possible AI security capabilities that disproportionately advantage defenders.

If you don't like what this means for attacker access to models, I agree with you!  The answer is to solve the quadratic coordination problem among cyber organizations, AI companies, governments, and Internet infrastructure providers by building institutions that identify attacker groups, kick them off inference platforms, and, wherever possible, get them arrested.  This is an operational threat intelligence / threat interdiction problem, not a trusted access program problem.
